analysis.one_liner: Bans requiring workers to join a union or pay union fees as a condition of employment nationwide.
analysis.headline: The national right-to-work bill never got a hearing or a vote: the Senate labor committee sat on it until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal labor law to ban "union security" agreements — the contracts that let employers require workers to pay union dues or fees as a condition of keeping their job. It would apply that ban nationwide, in every state, under both the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act. The bill never advanced past its first day: it was referred to the Senate labor committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees who object to financially supporting a union would keep that money while still receiving union-negotiated wages and contract coverage, since federal law requires unions to represent every worker in a bargaining unit. Employers would also gain: unions, cut off from fee revenue, would have fewer resources for bargaining, organizing, and policing contracts. About half the states already ban these fees, so the bill's practical effect would fall on unionized workplaces in the remaining states.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the provisions of federal law that let a union and an employer sign a contract requiring workers to join the union or pay dues and fees to keep their job, in both the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act

For employers, weakens the financial footing of unions they bargain with: unions would remain legally required to represent every worker in a covered unit while losing the ability to charge most of those workers for the cost, which shrinks union treasuries and bargaining capacity

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions, which would lose dues and fee revenue nationwide while still being legally obligated to represent every worker in a bargaining unit, and the workers who rely on union bargaining power for wages, benefits, and contract enforcement — a smaller, poorer union negotiates from a weaker position.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a free-rider problem: unions must bargain for and represent every worker in a covered unit, but could no longer require any of them to pay for that representation, so the cost of collective bargaining falls on fewer members until the union shrinks

Weaker unions mean weaker bargaining over wages and benefits; states with these bans have generally shown lower union membership and lower wages in unionized sectors, so the individual savings on dues come partly out of the pay the union negotiates

The bill overrides state policy choices in both directions — it would also strip payroll-deduction arrangements for railroad workers that current federal law specifically allows, replacing negotiated arrangements with a single federal mandate

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The individual gain is real but small: a worker who resents paying fees keeps that money. The collective cost is larger and falls on the same group, because the bill cuts union funding while leaving unions' legal duty to represent everyone intact — a mechanism that reliably shrinks unions and weakens the bargaining that produced the wages in the first place. An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill's main practical effect is fewer, weaker unions rather than merely freer workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's labor committee, which never gave it a hearing or a vote, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the National Right-to-Work Act on March 7, 2017, joined by 30 Republican cosponsors, making the bill's entire support Republican
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the standard first step
No further action ever appears on the bill's record: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote. It sat in committee until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and expired

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions kept the existing rules that let them negotiate fee requirements, and the workers whose pay and benefits depend on union bargaining were spared a nationwide weakening of it. The employers who backed the bill gained nothing from the outcome.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate

for.name: 30 of 52 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat or independent did

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee with no action after referral

against.name: AFL-CIO and organized labor
against.what_they_did: Opposed national right-to-work legislation as a union-destroying measure

sides.party_line_note: All 31 Senate supporters — sponsor plus 30 cosponsors — were Republicans, and the bill never reached a floor vote where the broader split could be measured.

industries.note: Unions would lose the ability to charge fees to the workers they are legally required to represent, cutting their funding nationwide. Because union bargaining sets pay, benefits, and grievance protection for millions of workers, the union's interest here largely runs with the workers it represents.

industries.industry: Unionized employers (manufacturing, airlines and railroads, construction, transit)
industries.note: Employers would bargain with unions that have smaller treasuries and shrinking membership, lowering labor costs and weakening organized labor's leverage over wages and working conditions. The gain comes directly out of workers' collective bargaining position.
